=== FINDING 1 (the important one): THE RULE GATES ON REPO FACTS IT NEVER USES, AND IS THEREFORE UNCONDITIONALLY INERT ON THE CODEX ADAPTER -- INCLUDING AT deny ===
The module docstring says it plainly: "The one use of `event.repo` is a presence/completeness gate, not a field this rule consumes for its own logic." That is accurate -- I grepped evaluate() and the ONLY repo references are `repo is None` and `repo.facts_incomplete`. Classification reads `event.tool_input`; authorisation reads `config.options`. The rule needs NOTHING from RepoFacts to reach its verdict.

Yet evaluate() returns None the moment `repo is None` or `repo.facts_incomplete`. MEASURED directly against the real module:
    mode=warn  repo=None              -> SILENT (None)
    mode=warn  facts_incomplete=True  -> SILENT (None)
    mode=warn  facts gathered         -> FINDING mode=warn
    mode=deny  repo=None              -> SILENT (None)
    mode=deny  facts_incomplete=True  -> SILENT (None)
    mode=deny  facts gathered         -> FINDING mode=deny
Consequences, in order of seriousness:
  (a) The Codex adapter gathers no repo facts (I checked: no RepoFacts/repo_facts reference anywhere under adapters/codex/, and the docstring says so). So this rule NEVER FIRES AT ALL under Codex -- not at warn, not at deny -- despite having the command string and the policy, i.e. everything it needs. That is not a parsing blind spot; it is the whole rule switched off for one of the product's two adapters. The docstring's "Known, accepted blind spots" list is entirely about command-shape under-matching and does NOT include "inert on Codex".
  (b) In DENY mode this is the exact fail-open shape build-plan item 1.2 exists to remove -- "today it permits when it cannot read git, advertising enforcement it cannot deliver" -- and PR #51 is IN FLIGHT right now removing it from lwb_proof_required. D9 names this rule the plan's SECOND deny-capable rule. So the moment someone arms it, it ships the defect 1.2 just finished closing next door.
  (c) The behaviour is LOCKED IN BY A TEST: tests/core/test_lwb_no_unauthorised_destructive_action.py:254, test_repo_none_is_silent_even_when_policy_would_otherwise_deny, asserts silence at DENY. Its docstring says the rule "is not allowed to fabricate a repo-facts-dependent opinion it cannot honestly have" -- but the opinion is NOT repo-facts-dependent, by the module's own admission. The test's stated premise is false about its own rule, which is what makes this worth writing down rather than leaving as taste.
The docstring justifies the gate as "mirroring lwb_proof_required's discipline exactly." That justification does not transfer: lwb_proof_required NEEDS repo facts (it must look for a proof record, so absent facts really do mean "could not check"). This rule does not. Suppressing a judgement you are fully able to make is not the same virtue as refusing to invent one you cannot -- and collapsing the two is, ironically, a cousin of the very defect pattern HANDOFF.md item 5 names.
NOT BLOCKING, because the rule ships at "warn" in core/policy/default.json and a warn that does not fire is noise-free, not unsafe. But this MUST be resolved in the deny-arming item, and the fix is small: drop the repo gate entirely (the rule does not need it), or keep it only for whatever future logic actually consumes RepoFacts.

=== FINDING 2: THE CLASSIFIER OVER-MATCHES, CONTRADICTING ITS OWN STATED BIAS -- INCLUDING ON THE RECOVERY COMMAND ===
The docstring is explicit: "Parsing posture: UNDER-match, deliberately ... a false positive trains people to ignore this gate within a week." I ran a classification matrix against the real module. Correct and silent, as designed: `git merge origin/main`, `gh pr merge 53 --squash`, `git push origin main`, `echo 'git push --force'` (quote-blanking works -- no false positive), and the two documented blind spots (`git -C /tmp push --force`, `gh api -X DELETE .../git/refs/heads/x`). Correct and firing: all three force-push forms, `git push origin --delete X`, `git push origin :X`, `gh api -X PATCH repos/o/r`, `gh api -X DELETE repos/o/r/rulesets/1`, `gh repo delete o/r`, `git filter-branch`, `git commit --amend`.
But these three fire as `history_rewrite` and should not:
    git rebase --abort      -> history_rewrite   <-- ABORTING a rebase UNDOES a rewrite; it is the recovery action
    git rebase --continue   -> history_rewrite   <-- mid-operation continuation, the rewrite was already authorised or not at `git rebase`
    git reset --hard        -> history_rewrite   (and `git reset --hard HEAD`, same)
The last one matters most in practice: bare `git reset --hard` / `git reset --hard HEAD` is the single most common "discard my working-tree changes" command and rewrites NO history whatsoever -- it moves HEAD nowhere. The implementation is `if sub == "reset" and "--hard" in tokens[2:]` with no look at the target, and `if sub == "rebase"` with no look at the operation flag. That is the "reads one field, ignores the sibling that changes its meaning" shape.
None of this is disclosed: the docstring's blind-spot list is under-match only, docs/rules/lwb-no-unauthorised-destructive-action.md's table lists `git reset --hard` as in-scope but says nothing about `--abort`/`--continue` or the bare form, and the only test is the parametrised `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, which IS a genuine history discard. So the over-match surface is undocumented AND untested.
At warn this is noise. Armed to deny, blocking `git rebase --abort` would trap someone mid-rebase with the gate forbidding the way out -- which is worse than the violation it is guarding. Suggested fix, small: exclude `--abort`/`--continue`/`--skip` from the rebase match, and require `git reset --hard` to name a target other than HEAD (or drop bare `reset --hard` and keep `reset --hard <commit-ish>`).
NOT BLOCKING at warn -- surfacing exactly this kind of thing is what the warn period is for -- but it should be fixed before arming.

I CONSIDERED DISAGREE ON FINDING 2 AND DECIDED AGAINST IT, and say so rather than leaving the reasoning invisible: `git rebase --abort` warning is a real classifier bug, not taste, and it is cheap to fix. What held me back is proportion -- the rule ships at warn, nothing is enforced, no data is at risk, the PR is already the re-cut of a re-cut, and this repo has shown that each extra cycle costs stale records and re-cuts of its own. A DISAGREE here would buy a one-line fix at the price of another full cycle. I record the finding with the patch shape instead, and if the owner reads it the other way, that is a legitimate call I would not argue with.
